questions.q: Which relational algebra operation selects the tuples (rows) that satisfy a given condition?
questions.explanation: Selection (σ) filters rows using a predicate, for example σ age>18 (Student). Projection (π) picks columns, not rows.

questions.q: Which operation picks only the required attributes (columns) and removes duplicate tuples from the result?
questions.explanation: Projection keeps the chosen columns. Since a relation is a set of tuples, rows that become identical after dropping columns appear only once.

questions.q: Relation R has 4 tuples and relation S has 5 tuples. How many tuples does the Cartesian product R × S contain?
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S, so it has 4 × 5 = 20 tuples. The number 9 would be 4 + 5.

questions.q: Two relations R and S are union-compatible, so R ∪ S is allowed, when:
options: They have the same number of tuples
They have a common primary key
They have the same number of attributes with compatible domains
questions.explanation: Union, intersection and set difference need the same number of attributes with matching domains. The number of tuples does not matter.

questions.q: Which of the following operations can be expressed using the other operations and is therefore not a fundamental operation?
questions.explanation: Intersection can be written as R ∩ S = R − (R − S). Union, set difference, Cartesian product, selection, projection and rename are the fundamental operations.

questions.q: The natural join R ⋈ S is equivalent to:
options: A Cartesian product, then a selection on equality of the common attributes, then a projection that removes the duplicate columns
A union of R and S followed by a projection
A selection on R followed by a set difference with S
A Cartesian product without any selection
questions.explanation: Natural join pairs tuples of R and S that have equal values on all common attributes and keeps only one copy of each common column.

questions.q: The division operator (R ÷ S) is best suited for queries of the type:
options: Find students who enrolled in at least one course
Find students who have enrolled in ALL the courses of a given set
Find students who enrolled in no course
Find the total number of students
questions.explanation: Division answers ‘for all’ queries, such as students who took every course listed in S. At-least-one queries need only a join or selection.

questions.q: A left outer join of R and S returns:
options: Only the tuples that have a match in both R and S
Only the tuples of S that have no match in R
The Cartesian product of R and S
All tuples of R, with NULLs in the attributes of S where there is no matching tuple
questions.explanation: A left outer join keeps every tuple of the left relation. When there is no matching tuple in S, the attributes of S are filled with NULL. An inner join would drop such tuples.

questions.q: A hash join can be used only for:
questions.explanation: A hash join splits tuples into partitions using a hash of the join attribute, so tuples with equal values land together. It cannot handle conditions such as R.a < S.b.

questions.q: In tuple relational calculus, a query has the form {t | P(t)}. It means:
options: The set of all tuples t for which the predicate P(t) is true
Return t only if P is a primary key
Delete every tuple t that satisfies P
questions.explanation: A tuple calculus query describes WHAT result is wanted (all tuples t that satisfy P), not the steps to compute it.

questions.q: In domain relational calculus the variables range over:
options: Values from the domains of attributes
questions.explanation: Domain calculus variables stand for single attribute values. In tuple calculus the variables stand for whole tuples.

questions.q: In query evaluation, pipelining means:
options: Writing every intermediate result to disk before the next operation starts
Running the query on several computers
Passing the output tuples of one operation directly to the next operation without storing the whole intermediate result
questions.explanation: Materialization stores each intermediate result as a temporary relation on disk. Pipelining passes tuples on as they are produced, which saves disk writes and reads.

questions.q: A tuple relational calculus expression is called safe when:
options: It uses only the AND connective
It never refers to a primary key
questions.explanation: An expression such as {t | NOT (t ∈ Student)} would return infinitely many tuples, so it is unsafe. Safe expressions always give a finite answer.

questions.q: Which SQL clause is used to filter groups after GROUP BY has been applied?
questions.explanation: HAVING applies a condition to groups, for example HAVING COUNT(*) > 5. WHERE works on individual rows before grouping.

questions.q: What is the main difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after aggregation
HAVING filters rows before grouping, WHERE filters groups
WHERE can be used only with joins
questions.explanation: WHERE cannot use aggregate functions such as COUNT or AVG, because it runs before the groups exist. HAVING runs after grouping and can use them.

questions.q: A table has 10 rows and 3 of them contain NULL in the column Marks. What does SELECT COUNT(Marks) return?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) ignores NULL values, so it counts 10 − 3 = 7. COUNT(*) would count all 10 rows.

questions.q: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from the result of a SELECT query?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each different row only once. ALL keeps duplicates, and UNIQUE is a constraint on a column, not a query keyword for results.

questions.q: Which condition correctly finds the rows where the column Phone has no value?
questions.explanation: NULL is not equal to anything, not even to another NULL, so = NULL never matches. The correct test is IS NULL.

questions.q: Which statement adds a new column to an existing table?
options: UPDATE TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(50)
ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(50)
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE changes the structure of a table, including adding a column. UPDATE changes row values, not the structure.

questions.q: Which of the following was introduced with SQL3 (SQL:1999)?
options: Recursive queries, triggers and user-defined types
questions.explanation: SQL:1999 (SQL3) added object-relational features: recursive queries, triggers, user-defined types and procedural extensions.

questions.q: What does SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Emp GROUP BY dept; return?
options: The total number of rows of Emp only
All rows of Emp sorted by dept
The department with the largest count only
One row per department with the number of employees in it
questions.explanation: GROUP BY makes one group per department, and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group, giving one result row per department.

questions.q: Which of the following is an open source DBMS?
questions.explanation: MySQL (like PostgreSQL) is open source. Oracle Database, DB2 and SQL Server are commercial products, although free editions of them exist.

questions.q: DB2 is a relational database product of:
questions.explanation: DB2 is developed by IBM. Oracle Database belongs to Oracle Corporation and SQL Server to Microsoft.

questions.q: The functional dependency X → Y holds in a relation if:
options: Y is a subset of the primary key
Any two tuples that have the same value for X also have the same value for Y
X and Y have different domains
X is a foreign key referring to Y
questions.explanation: X → Y means that the value of X decides the value of Y. For example, RollNo → Name: two rows with the same roll number must have the same name.

questions.q: The Armstrong axiom of reflexivity says that:
options: If X → Y then XZ → YZ
If X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z
If Y is a subset of X then X → Y
If X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ
questions.explanation: Reflexivity gives the trivial dependencies: a set of attributes always determines its own subsets. The other options are augmentation, transitivity and the union rule.
